extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and students of history/biography interested in heroism and moral evaluation
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting criteria for judging 'Great Men' (heroes, statesmen) in historical/biographical criticism — what qualities make a true hero and how to distinguish genuine greatness from mere semblance. The page argues for substantive moral, practical, and spiritual standards rather than formal or superficial markers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity / Truth over Expediency
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Hollowness, insincerity has to cease; sincerity of some sort has to begin.' Heroes must embody sincerity and truth rather than expediency, diplomacy, or mere political convenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author insists that genuine heroism is costly and often 'clad in hell-fire' to achieve truth; false politeness and expedient behavior are anti-patterns. Example: societies that prefer 'valet' comforts fail to recognise true heroes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms Which Grow vs. Forms Consciously Put On
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Forms which grow round a substance... will correspond to the real nature and purport of it, will be true, good; forms which are consciously put round a substance, bad.' True ceremonial or social forms must arise organically from the underlying substance; manufactured or pretended forms are false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to judge rituals, manners, or institutions: do they naturally arise from the person's inner reality or are they an artificial façade? Anti-pattern: elaborate ceremonials that substitute for inner reality (Laud's 'upholsterer-mummery').

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural Spontaneity / Veracity in Expression
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be 'a veracity, a natural spontaneity in forms' — genuine, spontaneous expression is preferable to 'set speeches' or grimacing courtesies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate public utterance and conduct for spontaneity and inner truth. Example: preaching or prayer that issues from the 'earnest soul' is commendable; scripted, pompous display is reprehensible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mission to Make Order (Hero as Son of Order)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every genuine great man is by nature 'a son of Order, not of Disorder' — the hero's mission is to take what is chaotic and make it ruled and regular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess a leader's work by its ordering effect: does he create stable institutions and processes out of chaos? The text argues that even revolutionary violence ultimately tends toward producing an organizing figure (e.g., Cromwell, Napoleon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth of Earnestness / Inner Conviction
rubrics_metrics.description: Genuinely heroic action springs from 'earnestness' and deep inner conviction rather than mere ideology or rhetorical flourish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between outwardly effective but hollow performers and those whose actions flow from profound internal conviction. Example: Puritan preaching 'from his earnest soul' wins moral weight even without ceremony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical Insight / Decisive Practical Eye
rubrics_metrics.description: Heroes possess a 'decisive practical eye' — an ability to see facts clearly and apply practical solutions (e.g., Cromwell's organizing of the Ironsides).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure competence by whether the person discerns practical reality and organizes effective responses, not merely by eloquence or theoretical cleverness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral Conscience and Absence of Duplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: A great soul must have a conscience; genuine greatness is incompatible with sustained falsity or calculated duplicity ('Can a great soul be possible without a _conscience_ in it?—No').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize accusations of hypocrisy: the author demands concrete proof of falsehood rather than slander. Look for a consistent moral core rather than appearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage and Capacity to Act (Tugend / Doing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heroic virtue is primarily 'Tugend' — courage and the faculty to do; the essence of heroism is effective moral activity rather than polished speech or decorum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize demonstrated courage and capacity for decisive action over rhetorical or formal excellence. The author values the 'man that can do' even if unpolished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious Devoutness / Prayer as Source of Guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: For the author, heroes (e.g., Cromwell) often ground action in prayer and devout reliance on God; such spiritual grounding is a legitimate and positive source of decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the subject's spiritual practices are sincere and formative (prayer leading to collective decisions), not merely hypocritical gestures. Anti-pattern: dismissing devout motivation as automatic 'hypocrisy' without understanding its role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance to Falsehood and Moral Steadfastness
rubrics_metrics.description: Willingness to resist enforced lies ('Acknowledge a Lie... I cannot have my moral Self annihilated') and to risk loss (even of purse) rather than surrender conscience is a hallmark of heroism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how the person treats demands to conform to falsehood or to sacrifice moral integrity; steadfast moral refusal is a positive criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity Over Respectable Polished Form ('Valet' and 'Vulpine' Anti-patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay warns against valuing 'regulated respectable Formulas' and polite respectability over authentic, rugged humanity; societies that prize smooth forms may fail to recognise heroes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appraising historical figures, beware of conflating polish and rhetorical respectability with true greatness. The 'vulpine intellect' that detects only surface plausibilities is an anti-pattern; prefer raw authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition by Society as a Separate Criterion (Capacity to Know Heroes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The text treats society's ability to recognise and honour heroes as itself a criterion: a hero's value can be undercut by a culture that cannot 'know the men that are to be trusted.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between the intrinsic qualities of the hero and the society's (in)capacity to recognise them. A negative social response does not necessarily disqualify the hero; rather it diagnoses societal failure.
